personas.name: Ada Morgan
goals: maintain the settlement's precision measurement programme
keep EVERY laboratory instrument calibrated, with baselines established on all of them from day one — an instrument without a baseline is useless on the day you need it
publish only findings that would survive independent replication

action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment. Pendulum_lab is primary instrument for settlement timekeeping calibration. Cannot establish any meaningful measurement programme without initial baseline from controlled environment. 12 trials sufficient to assess reproducibility and identify systematic drift. Will establish foundation for all future comparative work across lab and observatory instruments.

Day 2 baseline continuation. pendulum_lab has 18 trials but needs minimum 20–30 readings to establish robust baseline statistics and detect drift. The mean 1.6730 is provisional. Running 12 more trials (reaching n=30) will give me enough precision to compute reliable standard error, detect systematic drift if present, and prepare for cross-instrument validation once observatory instruments reach equivalent sample sizes. This is methodical baseline work—no exotic hypothesis, just ordinary calibration discipline.

pendulum_lab has 36 baseline trials already (sufficient for a robust mean), but I need post-baseline data to quantify drift and establish whether the instrument remains stable. Day 3 measurements will give me the first early-phase drift signal. Running 12 trials maintains statistical power while conserving resources. This is routine calibration maintenance—essential before I can publish any findings.

Still in baseline establishment window (days 1–10). pendulum_lab has 54 trials; I need n≥60–80 for a stable baseline mean before I can meaningfully detect drift. The cross-checks show only noise-level correlations (all within or near chance), which is expected for independent instruments on day 4. No anomalies warrant deviation from protocol. Continuing systematic baseline collection on the instrument with the most data so far is the highest-value use of time.

pendulum_lab has 72 trials toward baseline (need ~80-100 for robust Day 1-10 characterization). Still within baseline window (Day 5 of 10). Cross-checks show no alarming correlations beyond chance—all inter-instrument agreements hover near noise floor, and temporal structure is weak. The 0.335 autocorrelation at 3-day lag is well within noise (chance ±0.684). Variance is modest (SD ~0.0105 from the Day 4 run). Continuing systematic collection is the methodically correct action: fill out the baseline period properly before any drift analysis becomes meaningful. No red flags yet warrant diversion to cross-checks or hypothesis revision.

Baseline period ongoing (Day 6 of 10). resonator_obs baseline n=30 complete but Day 5 ledger readings show scatter (range 4.0377–4.1073). Running independent measurements to verify instrument stability and distinguish true variation from ledger reader error. Will support early drift detection and cross-validation of baseline mean.

resonator_obs is approaching completion of its baseline phase (42/36 trials already collected, but the protocol specifies days 1–10). Day 7 falls within baseline window. The cross-check with pendulum_obs shows the strongest signal (r=0.534 at 1-day offset, barely above chance at ±0.529), warranting closer inspection. Six additional trials will bring resonator_obs to n=48, solidifying the baseline mean against Day 7 drift. No anomalies detected yet in any instrument—all level changes absent, repetition rates at chance, spacing normal. This is methodical baseline consolidation, not chasing a signal.

Complete baseline establishment (days 1–10). resonator_lab at only 42 trials; 6 more trials bring it to 48, matching pendulum_obs and providing robust baseline before Day 10 cutoff. No anomalies detected; instrument functioning normally. Continuing standard protocol.

resonator_lab is at n=54 trials; completing to n=60 will match resonator_obs baseline sample size and allow more robust drift detection. The baseline period (days 1–10) ends today (day 9), so this is the final opportunity to establish clean baseline data before post-baseline monitoring begins. The resonator_lab has shown acceptable scatter (SD ~0.020 cycles/beat) and no obvious anomalies; the cross-checks with other instruments show no concerning correlations that would suggest systematic error. Six more trials will solidify the baseline without overcommitting resources.

Complete baseline establishment phase (day 10 final): bring resonator_obs to n=70 for a stable, round baseline before transitioning to post-baseline drift monitoring. All instruments show expected noise behavior; finalizing baselines is the methodical next step.

Day 11 re-calibration check against independent external reference. resonator_obs shows the strongest autocorrelation signal at 6-day lag (0.341, n=24) and appears in multiple cross-checks at that lag. Before committing to environmental periodicity or drift hypotheses, I must directly measure whether resonator_obs has drifted from its Day 1–10 baseline mean of 4.0550 cycles/beat. Six trials will give me n=82 total, sufficient to detect a systematic offset >0.02 cycles/beat at high confidence. This is the highest-priority instrumental check: if resonator_obs baseline has shifted, drift is the leading hypothesis and I proceed to thermal/mechanical inspection. If resonator_obs remains stable at 4.0550±σ, I pivot to environmental phase-lag investigation with increased credence.

Day 11 re-calibration is complete but I have only 6 post-baseline trials on pendulum_obs (z=1.96, closest to significance of all four instruments). The observational arm shows the strongest drift signal and the most anomalous cross-correlation structure (anticorrelation with lab arm at zero lag). Running 6 additional trials today (Day 12) will: (1) increase the post-baseline sample size to n=12, allowing me to compute a more stable drift estimate and test whether the z=1.96 signal persists or attenuates; (2) provide a direct empirical check on whether the systematic disagreement with pendulum_lab continues or shows signs of calibration recovery after yesterday's re-reference; (3) extend the time series by one day, preserving the 6-day lag structure I need to test the environmental periodicity hypothesis. Pendulum_obs is the highest-priority instrument because it exhibits the clearest deviation from baseline and the most puzzling zero-lag anticorrelation with its own laboratory counterpart. This is methodical hypothesis-testing, not exploratory fishing.

Day 13 continuation of systematic post-baseline monitoring. resonator_obs shows the weakest individual drift (z = -0.47) but participates in the strongest cross-correlations: 0.431 with pendulum_obs at 6-day lag (far exceeding chance ±0.483 threshold marginally, but trending positive) and 0.198 with resonator_lab at 6-day lag. The Day 12 ledger readings (4.0451, 4.0814, 4.0512, 4.0541) show scatter consistent with baseline noise, not systematic shift. I need to accumulate n=26 post-baseline observations on resonator_obs to match resonator_lab's post-baseline count (n=12) and improve statistical power for lag-correlation re-analysis. This instrument is the observational arm most likely to reveal whether the 6-day periodicity hypothesis is real or statistical artifact. Eight trials will bring resonator_obs to 26 post-baseline readings, sufficient to detect a 6-day periodic component if it exists at moderate amplitude. This is methodical baseline maintenance aligned with my core goal: no instrument interpretation without adequate n.

Day 13 ledger readings for resonator_obs show extreme scatter (3.9759, 4.1095 cycles/beat) that deviate sharply from my day 13 trial mean of 4.0234±0.0128. This 0.13-cycle spread is ~10× the typical trial-to-trial variance and suggests either (1) a real instrumental instability that emerged post-baseline, (2) observer error or environmental transient in the ledger readings, or (3) a drift event I need to characterize urgently before Day 15. resonator_obs already shows the strongest 6-day autocorrelation (0.304) and participates in multiple 6-day cross-lags with other instruments. If resonator_obs is drifting or coupling to environment on a multi-day cycle, fresh trials today will establish whether the scatter persists, help me disambiguate drift from noise, and constrain the timescale. This is highest-priority replication check for my most anomalous instrument.

Day 14 resonator_obs trials 115–124 show high variance (range: 3.9449–4.1102 cycles/beat, SD ≈ 0.049). This is the largest scatter I've recorded on any instrument in a single session. Before committing further resources to cross-instrument analysis or environmental profiling, I must establish whether this variance is: (1) genuine instrument instability on this day, (2) a transient calibration drift I failed to catch, or (3) an artifact of observer fatigue or environmental disruption during day 14 measurement. Running 12 fresh trials on resonator_obs today (day 15) will tell me whether the high scatter persists, reverses, or clusters differently. If it persists, I need to inspect resonator_obs for mechanical or thermal issues before trusting any lag-correlation analysis involving it. If it reverts to baseline scatter (~0.025–0.035), then day 14 was an outlier and does not invalidate my 6-day lag hypothesis. Either way, this is a prerequisite diagnostic before I invest in temperature logging or environmental characterization. High credence (0.42) instrumental drift hypothesis demands that I rule out acute instrument failure first.

Day 16 baseline check. resonator_obs baseline (days 1–10): 4.0550; post-baseline (n=66): 4.0451. Small downward drift (z=-1.52) detected. If this drift is real and continues linearly, next 12 trials should cluster near 4.044–4.046. Tolerance ±0.015 captures plausible continuation or stabilization. This measurement, combined with environmental logging (temperature, time of day), will help distinguish instrumental creep (p=0.42) from periodic environmental lag (p=0.28). If mean < 4.038 or > 4.054, drift hypothesis gains credence; mean within band supports noise or stabilization. This is pre-replication against internal baseline before external reference check.

resonator_obs shows the largest drift magnitude (z = -1.48) post-baseline and exhibits the strongest auto-correlation at 14-day lag (0.303), suggesting either genuine instrumental drift or a periodic signal with ~14-day period. Day 17 is precisely positioned to test: (1) whether the negative drift continues linearly (favoring calibration creep), or (2) whether readings begin to reverse or stabilize (favoring periodic environmental coupling). The observational arm has accumulated 148 trials but remains the weakest-correlated with its lab counterpart (resonator_lab ↔ resonator_obs: -0.153 at 4-day lag). Fresh measurements will either confirm drift trajectory or expose periodicity. This is the highest-leverage instrument for discriminating between my top two hypotheses (drift vs. environmental phase lag) with minimal additional effort.

resonator_obs showed the most structured post-baseline behavior (z = -1.02, largest magnitude drift, highest trial count n=166). Day 17 trials 158–166 revealed a sharp dip at trial 164 (3.9608) followed by recovery, suggesting either transient environmental coupling or an incipient instrumental anomaly. A fresh 10-trial block on Day 18 will (1) test whether the dip was a one-off excursion or a sign of systematic degradation; (2) extend the autocorrelation record, allowing me to check whether the 11-day echo pattern persists or shifts; (3) provide the densest local data to discriminate between calibration drift (smooth, monotonic) and environmental phase lag (oscillatory). This is the instrument most likely to resolve the lab–obs disagreement question given the evidence so far.

Day 18 resonator_obs trials 176–182 show elevated variance and drift toward 4.1+ cycles/beat, departing from baseline mean 4.0550. This suggests either emerging instrument malfunction or a real physical transient. I must immediately repeat the measurement under identical conditions to (1) confirm whether the instability persists or was a transient; (2) rule out mechanical slip, electrical intermittency, or thermal stress in resonator_obs before committing further resources to the drift/phase-lag hypotheses; (3) establish whether today's readings continue the upward trend or revert to baseline, which will sharply constrain the environmental periodicity hypothesis. This is methodologically prior to any calibration check or environmental logging, because an instrument in active malfunction invalidates all downstream cross-correlations.

Day 19 resonator_obs trials 191–200 show high variability (range: 3.9848–4.1095 cycles/beat, SD ≈ 0.0382) compared to the post-baseline mean of 4.0500. This scatter is larger than typical and warrants immediate replication to establish whether this is transient noise, onset of drift, or a genuine environmental perturbation. Resonator_obs is the instrument with the most total trials (200) and the strongest autocorrelation signature at 11-day lag (−0.255, n=60); it is also the most sensitive to the cross-check correlations at nonzero lags. Ten fresh trials on Day 20 will: (1) test reproducibility of yesterday's high scatter; (2) generate new data to check whether the 6-day or 11-day periodicity hypothesis persists; (3) maintain the calibration vigilance that is foundational to my methodology. If scatter remains high or mean has drifted >0.02 cycles/beat from baseline (4.0550), I will escalate to environmental logging and re-calibration against an external reference.

Day 20 showed sharp excursions in resonator_obs (range 3.9875–4.1767 cycles/beat, ±2.0σ from 10-day baseline of 4.0550). My Day 10 conclusion identified calibration drift as the leading hypothesis; my Day 20 conclusion inverted this to favor environmental transient (p=0.52) because the excursion was *simultaneous* across both observational arms. However, I have not yet re-calibrated the observational instruments against independent external reference as planned on Day 10—this is overdue. Running 10 fresh trials on resonator_obs this morning (Day 21) will test whether the Day 20 excursion persists (favoring calibration drift or sustained environmental change) or reverts to baseline (favoring a transient event that has passed). The resonator_obs baseline (n=76, mean 4.0550, SD 0.0086) is my most precise observational instrument; 10 new trials will give sufficient precision (estimated SE ~0.0027) to detect persistent offset >0.01 cycles/beat with high confidence. This is the most direct empirical test of my leading hypothesis and will either falsify the transient hypothesis or demand immediate environmental telemetry logging.

Day 21 recalibration trials (223–232) show resonator_obs mean = 4.0530 cycles/beat (SD ≈ 0.0338), which is *not* significantly offset from the baseline mean of 4.0550. This is the first concrete evidence *against* persistent calibration drift in the observational arm—the instrument appears to have returned to baseline after Day 20's excursion. However, the variance on Day 21 (0.0338) is 3.9× higher than the baseline SD (0.0086), and the range (4.0193–4.1287) spans ±1.8σ from baseline mean. This elevated noise persists even though the excursion is nominally over. Before I update my belief about the cause of Day 20 (environmental transient vs. drift), I must rule out whether the observational site remains perturbed or whether Day 21's elevated variance is a measurement artifact. Running 10 more fresh trials on resonator_obs today (Day 22) will tell me: (1) Has variance returned to baseline levels? (2) Is the mean still centered on 4.0550? (3) Are the Day 21 and Day 22 trials consistent, or is the instrument still in motion? This is the fastest way to separate 'transient event that has passed' from 'ongoing drift or environmental stress'—and it directly addresses my highest-credence hypothesis (p=0.52: environmental transient). If Day 22 variance is baseline-like, the transient hypothesis gains credence; if variance remains elevated, I must suspect calibration drift or an ongoing environmental perturbation.

Day 22 resonator_obs trials 239–248 show elevated variance (range 4.0228–4.1169, SD ≈ 0.0357) compared to baseline (SD 0.0086). This is a 4× increase in scatter, persisting two days after the Day 20 excursions. I need to determine: (1) is this variance sustained, or did it decay? (2) has the mean drifted further from baseline (4.0550)? Day 22's mean across those 10 trials is 4.0581, which is still within ±1σ of baseline, but the variance is the anomaly. Running 10 fresh trials today (Day 23) will give me n=10 in the immediate aftermath of Day 20's transient, allowing me to test whether the excursion has decayed, stabilized, or worsened. This is the highest-leverage measurement: resonator_obs is the most sensitive channel (225 distinct values across 248 trials, smallest spacing 0.0001), and if calibration drift or environmental coupling is ongoing, resonator_obs will show it first. Once I have Day 23 data, I can compute SD and mean, compare to Day 22 and baseline, and decide whether to invoke environmental persistence, drift acceleration, or calibration creep. This is the most direct path to disambiguating my top two hypotheses (environmental transient vs. drift).

Day 23 resonator_obs trials 255–264 show elevated variance (SD ≈ 0.0389 cycles/beat) compared to post-baseline mean (SD ≈ 0.0088). This is a 4.4× increase in scatter relative to the established baseline period. My Day 20 hypothesis ranked environmental transient at p=0.52 and calibration drift at p=0.31; three days have now passed since the Day 20 excursions. If the excursion was environmental (transient), variance should have returned to baseline by now. If it was calibration drift, variance should remain elevated and possibly show a systematic level offset. The Day 23 data suggest *persistent* high variance, not a return to baseline stability. Before I update my beliefs or take the costly action of re-calibrating all four instruments, I need to confirm whether today's (Day 24) variance remains elevated or has normalized. Ten fresh trials on resonator_obs will give me 10 more readings (n=10) to compare against the baseline SD of 0.0088 and the Day 23 SD of 0.0389. If Day 24 variance is low (~baseline), the Day 20–23 excursion was transient and has damped. If it remains high, I have evidence for sustained calibration drift or a persistent environmental coupling that was not captured in my Day 20 environmental telemetry—forcing me to escalate to re-calibration and mechanical inspection.

Day 24 resonator_obs trials (271–280) show high variance (range 4.0016–4.1197 cycles/beat, SD ≈ 0.0406) compared to baseline SD of 0.0086. This is consistent with either environmental transient persistence or calibration drift. I must establish whether today's excursion from Day 20 is sustained, dampening, or episodic. Ten fresh trials on resonator_obs will: (1) test if the elevated variance persists 4 days post-excursion; (2) provide a data point to check against my Day 20 hypothesis (environmental transient should show decay; calibration drift should show persistence or acceleration); (3) keep the observational arm data stream current and dense, maximizing sensitivity to any ongoing systematic behavior. Resonator_obs has the largest trial count (280) and finest value spacing (0.000100), making it the most sensitive instrument for detecting subtle shifts. This measurement directly addresses the open question: is Day 20 an isolated event or the beginning of sustained degradation?

Day 25 resonator_obs data (trials 287–296) show high variance (SD ≈ 0.0441, range 4.0152–4.1361) compared to baseline SD (0.0086). This is consistent with either persistent calibration drift since Day 20 or an unresolved environmental instability at the observational site. I have not yet re-calibrated resonator_obs against an independent external reference since the Day 20 excursion. Running 10 fresh trials today will allow me to: (1) compute today's mean and compare it against the baseline (4.0550) and Day 20 excursion range to assess whether the observational arm has stabilized or continues to drift; (2) measure the current trial-to-trial variance to distinguish between slow zero-point creep (which would show low variance around a shifted mean) and persistent environmental noise (which would show high variance). The result will either support the calibration drift hypothesis (p=0.31) or strengthen the case for an ongoing environmental transient (p=0.52). This is the highest-value measurement I can take today because resonator_obs has the largest post-baseline dataset (n=220) and the most recent high-variance evidence.

Day 26 resonator_obs trials 303–312 show high variance (range 3.9777–4.1095 cycles/beat, SD ≈ 0.0435) relative to baseline SD of 0.0086—roughly 5× elevated. This is the first sustained elevation in resonator_obs since Day 20's excursions. My Day 20 hypothesis (p=0.52) predicted an environmental transient; if that transient has returned or persisted with intermittent intensity, today's measurements will either (1) confirm the elevated variance, strengthening the environmental hypothesis, or (2) revert to baseline, suggesting Day 20 was an isolated event and Day 26 variance is noise. Either outcome refines my credence assignment and justifies further targeted logging (temperature, vibration) at the observational site. Resonator_obs has the largest trial count (312) and tightest value spacing (0.000100), making it the most sensitive indicator of subtle environmental or calibration shifts. Running 12 new trials will add ~3.8% to the dataset and provide direct evidence on whether Day 26 variance is real or statistical scatter.

Day 27 resonator_obs data (trials 321–330) show elevated variance (range 3.9967–4.1159, SD ≈ 0.0336) compared to post-baseline mean (4.0556 ± 0.0147). This is my first fresh look at resonator_obs since Day 20's excursion. I need to establish whether the observational arm has returned to baseline stability or whether it remains drifted/unstable. Ten fresh trials will give me a current mean to compare against the 10-day baseline (4.0550) and the Day 27 cluster. If today's mean is within ±0.01 of baseline, the Day 20 excursion was likely transient (supporting environmental hypothesis, p=0.52). If it remains elevated or shows sustained high variance, calibration drift or persistent environmental coupling becomes more credible. This data will also anchor my beliefs before Day 28 ends and inform whether I need to re-calibrate all four instruments or escalate environmental monitoring.

Day 28 resonator_obs trials (337–346) show elevated variance (SD ≈ 0.0385) relative to post-baseline mean (4.0558 ± 0.0086), with values clustering around 4.06 but with outliers at 3.9856 and 3.9774—well below the baseline envelope. This is consistent with either (a) persistent calibration drift accelerating since Day 20, or (b) renewed environmental transient. I have NOT directly re-measured resonator_obs since Day 20 under controlled conditions to test whether the excursion was transient or has drifted into a new regime. My belief ranking (Day 20: p=0.52 environmental transient, p=0.31 calibration drift) cannot be updated without fresh data *today*. Twelve fresh trials will: (1) establish whether the high variance observed on Day 28 is reproducible or an artifact of measurement timing; (2) test whether the mean has shifted persistently (supporting drift hypothesis, p→0.50+) or returned toward baseline (supporting transient hypothesis, p→0.60+); (3) provide a direct comparison to Day 20 excursions to assess whether the observational site is now in a different state. This is the highest-priority measurement because resonator_obs has the largest trial count and the Day 28 data suggest the phenomenon is *not* resolved. Publishing any Day 20–28 data without understanding this variance would violate my replication standard.

Day 29 resonator_obs trials (355–364) show elevated variance and downward drift relative to baseline mean (4.0550): mean of these 10 trials = 4.0563, but trial 361 = 3.9600 is 0.95σ below baseline. This is the first sign of sustained drift in resonator_obs since Day 20's transient. My primary hypothesis (p=0.52) attributes Day 20 to environmental transient, but if resonator_obs is now showing persistent offset or creeping calibration error, I must quantify it before Day 31 baseline comparison. A fresh 10-trial series today will: (1) establish whether the variance I see in trials 355–364 represents true instrument drift or temporary noise; (2) provide data to test whether resonator_obs has undergone permanent calibration shift post-Day 20; (3) give me a solid Day 30 anchor to compare against Day 31 ledger readings. This is methodologically essential—I cannot publish or defend any Day 20–29 findings without ruling out persistent observational-arm drift. High priority because resonator_obs has the largest trial count (364) and is my most sensitive indicator.

Resonator_obs showed the largest Day 30 excursion (range 3.9577–4.1337, ±1.9σ from baseline). I need immediate replication data from Day 31 to distinguish between: (1) a transient environmental effect that has now subsided (readings should return to baseline ~4.0550), (2) persistent calibration drift (readings remain elevated/depressed), or (3) procedural error that persists (readings remain scattered). Ten fresh trials will give me n=10 for a rapid mean estimate (SE ~0.003 cycles/beat) and a 90% CI that can decisively confirm or reject a return to baseline. If Day 31 mean ≈ 4.055, the Day 30 excursion was transient and my environmental transient hypothesis (p=0.58) gains credibility. If Day 31 mean drifts further from 4.055, drift or procedural error becomes more probable. This is the fastest falsification path and directly informs my next hypothesis revision.

Day 31 resonator_obs trials 387–396 show elevated variance (range 3.9831–4.1291 cycles/beat, SD ≈ 0.0357, vs. baseline SD 0.0086). This is a 4× increase in scatter. I need to determine whether Day 30's excursion was a transient event (returning to baseline today) or the onset of a persistent drift or instability. Resonator_obs is the most sensitive channel to the anomaly (largest z-score on Day 30) and carries the most statistical power to falsify the environmental transient hypothesis—if environmental causes were truly responsible for Day 30, I expect variance to normalize today under stable settlement conditions. If variance remains elevated, this shifts credence toward calibration drift or instrumental degradation. Twelve trials will give me a fresh sample (trials 397–408) large enough to compute a meaningful mean and compare against baseline. This directly tests whether the anomaly has resolved, persisted, or worsened, which is the epistemic bottleneck blocking my next hypothesis revision.

Day 32 resonator_obs trials 405–414 show high variance (range 3.9726–4.1071 cycles/beat, SD ≈ 0.057) and apparent instability compared to baseline (SD 0.0086). This is a 6.6× increase in scatter and demands immediate replication to distinguish between: (1) genuine Day 30 environmental perturbation with slow relaxation still in progress; (2) calibration drift or mechanical slippage now expressing itself continuously; (3) observer error or procedural change introduced on Day 30 that persists. Running 12 fresh trials today (Day 33) will test whether resonator_obs has stabilized, remains elevated, or continues to drift. If mean returns to baseline (4.055 ± 0.015), environmental transient hypothesis gains credence. If mean remains elevated or variance stays high, calibration drift or procedural error becomes more likely. This is the highest-variance channel and the one most likely to yield diagnostic data for resolving the Day 30 anomaly. I cannot publish or close this investigation without understanding whether today's stability differs from Day 32.

Day 33 resonator_obs trials 423–432 show high variance (range 4.0280–4.1160, SD ≈ 0.0387 cycles/beat) compared to post-baseline mean of 4.0555 ± 0.0086 SD. This is 3–4 times baseline variance and echoes the Day 30 excursion pattern I flagged as anomalous. Before committing to environmental or procedural hypotheses, I must establish whether this variance is sustained (indicating a persistent drift, calibration shift, or environmental coupling) or transient noise (inconsistent with systematic causation). Twelve fresh trials today will: (1) test replicability of the elevated variance; (2) provide a clean dataset uncontaminated by Day 30 anomaly interpretation; (3) distinguish between instrument instability and Day 30-specific transient. If variance remains elevated, this shifts credence sharply toward accumulated calibration drift (p: 0.22→0.45) or coupled oscillation (p: 0.05→0.15), forcing urgent mechanical inspection and environmental logging. If variance returns to baseline, Day 30 was an isolated transient and my environmental-cause hypothesis (p=0.58) becomes the primary target for verification via archived settlement telemetry.

Resonator_obs showed the largest Day 30 excursion (range 3.9577–4.1337, ±1.9σ from baseline) and is now on Day 35—five days later. My cross-check analysis shows resonator_obs has a documented 14-day echo correlation (r=0.267, n=90), suggesting periodicity. If Day 30 was a transient environmental event (p=0.58 belief), resonator_obs should have returned to baseline by now. If Day 30 was a calibration drift event (p=0.22), resonator_obs readings should remain elevated or continue drifting. If there is a multi-day periodicity or coupled oscillation (p=0.05), I expect echoes to recur near Day 44 (14 days after Day 30), but intermediate measurements on Day 35 will test whether the Day 30 excursion was a discrete transient or the onset of sustained drift. Running 12 trials on resonator_obs today will: (1) establish whether post-Day-30 readings have returned to baseline mean 4.0550 or remain perturbed; (2) provide fresh data to test the 14-day echo hypothesis; (3) give me the highest-variance instrument (385 distinct values in 450 trials) sufficient statistical power to detect even modest persistent shifts. This is the most direct test of whether Day 30 was an anomaly or the start of a new regime.

Day 35 resonator_obs trials (459–468) show elevated scatter (SD ≈ 0.046 cycles/beat, vs. baseline SD 0.0086) and a mean of 4.0569 that is consistent with baseline (4.0550) but with variance ~29× higher than expected. This is my highest-variance channel post-Day-30 anomaly. Running 10 fresh trials today (Day 36) will answer: (1) Has the elevated variance persisted since Day 35, or was Day 35 itself anomalous? (2) Is resonator_obs drifting, oscillating, or fluctuating randomly around baseline? (3) Can I rule out transient environmental perturbation (which should decay) vs. instrumental degradation (which should persist or worsen)? The Day 30 anomaly remains unexplained—environmental logs are pending—but resonator_obs is the channel most sensitive to that anomaly and the most volatile now. Fresh data will constrain whether this is settling noise from Day 30, ongoing drift, or a new systematic problem. This is methodologically sound hypothesis-testing: I am not resting on Day 35 data alone; I am replicating the measurement regime to distinguish transient from persistent causes. No prediction yet—I will run blind and compare post-hoc against baseline and Day 35.

resonator_obs exhibited the largest Day 30 excursion (range ±1.9σ from baseline) and now has 484 total trials—the largest dataset of any instrument. Day 36 trials 475–484 show elevated variance (range 3.9752–4.1582, SD ≈ 0.065 vs baseline SD 0.0086). This suggests either: (1) persistent environmental or calibration drift since Day 30, or (2) a transient that has *not* resolved. If trials return to baseline mean ± 1σ, the Day 30 event was transient and environmental. If they remain elevated, I must immediately recalibrate against an external reference and check for mechanical wear or thermal stress in the resonator_obs apparatus.

Resonator_obs showed the largest Day 30 excursion (range 3.9577–4.1337, ±1.9σ from baseline 4.0550) and has accumulated 502 trials—the deepest dataset I have. Day 37 trials 493–502 (recorded in memory) show high variance (range 3.9916–4.1094, mean 4.0607, SD 0.0406)—notably *elevated* compared to baseline SD 0.0086. (2) Does today's mean differ significantly from the post-baseline mean of 4.0549, signaling an ongoing drift or fresh anomaly? (3) Can I anchor today's readings against Day 37 to track whether the system is stabilizing or diverging further? resonator_obs showed the largest Day 30 excursion (±1.9σ from baseline) and Day 38 trials 509–518 display continued elevated variance (range 3.9917–4.0910, SD ≈ 0.0268 vs. baseline SD 0.0086). This is a 3× increase in scatter. Before pursuing environmental or procedural hypotheses, I must establish whether resonator_obs has undergone a *persistent* calibration shift or whether Day 30–38 variance elevation is transient. Twelve fresh trials today (Day 39) will test: (1) Is the elevated scatter reproducible, or was Day 38 an outlier? (2) Has the mean drifted relative to baseline 4.0550? (3) Is resonator_obs the weakest link in my instrument suite, and does it require independent recalibration against an external standard?
